articles.jina_text:
Land that borders a protected nature site is being investigated over claims it is being used as an illegal site to dump medical waste. 
The Environment Agency (EA) said it was investigating the site off Mill Lane, near Wadborough, in Worcestershire. The land is near Great Blaythorn Meadow, which is Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). 
A resident in the area, who asked not to be named, told the BBC a muck spreader, which are normally used to distribute farmyard manure, had been used to spread medical waste.
The EA said it was investigating alongside West Mercia Police, Wychavon District Council and Worcestershire County Council.
An EA spokesperson said: "Waste crime scars communities and the environment and, in line with our 10-point plan, we're acting quickly to tackle illegal activity."
The resident said they were concerned by how close the site was in relation to Great Blaythorn Meadow, which Natural England lists as an SSSI. 
Natural England considers the land special for its biological interest, specifically wanting to protect its rare lowland meadow and grassland habitat.

The resident claimed "local residents of Wadborough and Drakes Broughton had identified some of the spread waste as medical in origin" and "estimated that 300 tonnes of contaminated waste has been spread on the field".
However, the EA has not confirmed the nature of the waste or how much waste has been dumped.
Photos said to be taken at the scene show small scraps of metal and plastic scattered across the area which is under investigation.
In December 2025, the BBC revealed a site off Mill Lane was under investigation for illegal waste dumping.
At the time, it became the third site in Worcestershire being investigated for illegal waste dumping.
The others sites were Stone Arrow Farm, Peopleton and Haselor Lane, Evesham.
The EA said it was "pulling every lever available" to "disrupt those who profit from the harm illegal waste sites cause".

Drought conditions will continue until there is “sustained rainfall across the country”, the Environment Agency has said.




The public body said a “few days or even weeks of wetter weather cannot reverse the impacts of several months of exceptionally dry conditions”.








This summer was the first to see three separate days where temperatures exceeded 37C as parts of the country suffered as many as five heatwaves thought to have caused thousands of deaths.




August 28 to September 3 was the wettest week since early February, according to Environment Agency figures, with “rainfall improving river flows, soil moisture deficits and environmental conditions across much of England”.


The past week has seen rain in many parts of Britain – but not enough to ease drought conditions (PA)
PA Wire




However, reservoir storage continued to decline for several water companies as demand exceeded recharge, with the Environment Agency adding: “Further significant rainfall is needed to return to normal water resource conditions for many water companies.”




Reservoir storage fell to 58% nationally in Environment Agency data for the week ending September 1, remaining significantly below average, with 11 reservoirs less than half full.




The Environment Agency said farmers “face challenging conditions due to hard soil, especially where some abstraction restrictions remain that limit the availability of water to soften ground”.











River flows increased at many sites monitored by the agency at the start of the month, however some low flows continued in parts of the east and south-west England.




Some 10 areas of England were in drought status at the start of September: East Anglia; Hertfordshire and North London; Thames; Devon, Cornwall and Isles of Scilly; West Midlands; Wessex; Kent and South London; Solent and South Downs; East Midlands; Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire.







The remaining areas were in “prolonged dry weather status”, according to the Environment Agency.




Rainfall across August reached 78% of the long-term average nationally, although south-east England received only 54%.




The Met Office said autumn had marked a “significant change of weather type from summer, which was dominated by dry conditions”.

The Greens appeal to young and progressive voters here on defence, rent controls and North Sea oil. The Burnham bounce may be about to hit an obstacle





You might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right in Makerfield – can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?
For the Greens it matters almost existentially because failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster, was vacated (vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.



This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control and remained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.
A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinion makes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.
Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hill where Paddington Bear lives in the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given that only a quarter of residents are homeowners, compared with 62.5% across England and Wales.


Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure. The constituency is home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.

Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.
Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.

Syrian reactor could have been used for nuclear weapons if completed, UN says


Chief of nuclear watchdog says secret Assad-era facility would have been able to produce fissile material 




A nearly complete nuclear reactor built secretly during the rule of the toppled Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad would have been able to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the chief of the UN nuclear watchdog has revealed.
Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir ez-Zor and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities.

The IAEA head, Rafael Grossi, said on Monday it was “obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine” activities.
“They didn’t want the world to know what they were doing,” he told reporters after opening the Vienna-based agency’s quarterly board of governors meeting.

The cattle were culled by Mr Muir’s department on land near Fivemiletown, following a court order which disqualified the herd owner from keeping animals.




But concern was raised by some political representatives and farmers about the public nature of the incident and questions have been posed about whether all options were exhausted before the cows were shot.

Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average.

Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.
One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles. 
JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.

Big increases in wildfires and heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis are hindering improvements to air quality around the world, UN experts have said.
Regions that had recorded a fall in pollution emitted by cars and industrial sites are facing new threats to air quality because of exposure to smoke from wildfires, according to a new report, while rising temperatures caused by intense heatwaves are causing a surge in ground-level ozone.

In turn, the pollution generated by these climate-linked events is itself contributing to climate breakdown, creating a feedback loop that risks dragging the world deeper into environmental catastrophe.
“Air quality and climate cannot be treated as separate subjects; they are deeply intertwined and have to be treated together,” said Lorenzo Labrador, a scientific officer of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), which issued the report.

We’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same question

Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego





Our three cities are learning from each other about how to protect residents. These climate policies are also public health measures





This summer, mayors met in London during the heatwave that ironically threatened to derail London Climate Action Week.
As temperatures broke records across the UK and Europe, leading some climate talks to be suspended or cancelled, we found ourselves seeking shelter and comparing how our cities prepare for extreme heat: how we protect vulnerable residents, communicate risk, and redesign neighbourhoods for hotter summers.

At the same time, Paris was overseeing the city’s crisis response as another intense heatwave swept across France. Across Europe, more than 14,000 people lost their lives due to the heat.
As mayors, we are confronting the same question: how do you protect millions of people when extreme heat is no longer an exceptional event, but an increasingly familiar part of summer?
For Phoenix, that question has shaped city government for decades. For Paris and Milan, it is now becoming one of the defining challenges of urban leadership.






Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster
Michael Mann

Read more
It may strike some people as unusual that two of Europe’s oldest and most prestigious cities are looking to a city in the Arizona desert for ideas. But rising temperatures are now a global challenge, and we don’t have time for each city to figure out what works on its own.
Phoenix has learned, sometimes the hard way, that extreme heat cannot be treated as simply a weather event. It shapes decisions about transport, housing, public health, public space, and emergency planning. Preparing for summer begins long before temperatures start to rise.


Phoenix established one of the world’s first city offices dedicated to heat response and mitigation, reflecting an approach that focuses on both immediate relief from extreme heat, especially for those most vulnerable, and building resilience in the medium-long-term by implementing cooling solutions to make the city safer and more comfortable.
The city’s shade plans require 75% shade coverage in new development in areas with high pedestrian activity, and programs that support schools, transit users, and those most vulnerable. To further reduce the urban heat island effect, Phoenix is applying cool surface treatment to buildings and roadways, including on more than 300 kilometers of neighborhood streets.

The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.
Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.

If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts to reduce carbon emissions, one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to the World Resources Institute. Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).


Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they are generally poorer and they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.
The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today, according to the IEA. In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of 40% to 50% of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.
This is going to require a lot of energy. Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciences estimated that in India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.
This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to a United Nations report, about 7% of total emissions. articles.jina_text:
As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.
What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.
The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.
The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.
Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.
He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.
"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.
"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes with… to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

articles.jina_text:
Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.
The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.
But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.
There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show. 
Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.
An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.
The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.
Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."

However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.
"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.
The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.
"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."
The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.
Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department to consider de-listing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act and to contemplate whether the agency could make it easier to authorize killing them.
The order gives interior secretary Doug Burgum three months to determine whether gray wolves and Mexican gray wolves have recovered enough for the federal government to de-list them.

But the US Fish and Wildlife Service, a division of the interior department, has already attempted to de-list the gray wolf – a decision that is currently tied up in litigation. A 2022 federal court order has left wolves protected by the ESA across most of their range in the lower 48 states.
The major exception is in the northern Rocky Mountain states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming, where states manage wolves. In Minnesota, wolves are classified as “threatened” rather than “endangered”.
The USFWS has not attempted to de-list the Mexican gray wolf, a rare sub-species that was reintroduced to New Mexico and Arizona in 1998.
The current recovery plan for Mexican gray wolves requires a population average of more than 320 animals for four years in a row before federal authorities consider de-listing. Arizona and New Mexico counted a total of 319 animals at the end of 2025, triggering the first year in which officials can start counting to make the case for de-listing.
But Mexican gray wolves also face dire threats from lack of genetic diversity, according to Michael Robinson, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. Premature de-listing, he said, would likely invite challenge from environmental groups.
“We’re going to be fighting every step of the way, with information, with science,” Robinson said. “That should be the core of the decision-making process.”
Trump’s order also directs federal authorities to urge states to remove protections for gray wolves and loosen local restrictions on wolf killing.
The order drew sharp criticism from environmental groups.

The Met Office has warned the El Niño event developing over the Pacific is shaping up to be the most significant in living memory - and it will impact the weather in London over the coming months.




Forecasters have said that the phenomenon will cause the UK to experience more storms and rain over the coming autumn and winter.








It comes as Britons have been urged to stock up on food and water as the government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for emergencies. 




Environment secretary Angela Eagle told the Guardian: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.




“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”




An El Niño event is declared when sea surface temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise to 0.5C above the long-term average, impacting global rainfall patterns and average temperatures.












Current measurements show that they are over 2C above normal - and the Met Office is predicting that it could measure over 3C more than average later this year.




That would make this year’s weather event the largest since at least 1950, and possibly since the 19th century, according to the national forecaster.








Other climate groups have projected temperatures to even reach 4C above average.


People shelter from the rain under an umbrella, in Westminster, central London (Jonathan Brady/PA)
PA Wire


How will El Niño impact London’s weather?




The impact of such an event would mean that London, along with all of northwest Europe, would experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter.




El Niño can also increase the odds of cold weather late in the winter.




Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, said: “We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”

articles.title: Puffin numbers fall on Scottish island amid climate change concerns
articles.raw_rss: Experts said the drop on the Isle of May in the Firth of Forth is ‘disappointing’.
articles.raw_meta: Experts said the drop on the Isle of May in the Firth of Forth is ‘disappointing’.
articles.jina_text:
The number of puffins at one of the UK’s largest colonies has fallen by about 30% in the last two years, raising concerns for their future amid climate change.




Experts fear “extreme climate events”, including intense storms and marine heat waves, have had an impact on the birds’ survival rates in recent years.








NatureScot and the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) completed a count of burrows at the Isle of May National Nature Reserve (NNR) in the Firth of Forth this summer.




Scientists estimate that 36,500 puffin burrows were occupied, compared to 52,000 in the last survey in 2024, and 39,000 in 2017.


Puffins spend up to eight months of the year at sea (Owen Humphreys/PA)
PA Archive




NatureScot Isle of May reserve manager, David Steel, said: “This decline is disappointing and concerning.




“Puffin numbers on the island fell sharply in the 2000s and recovered in the 2010s but have now dropped again.




“The decrease appears to be linked to a combination of ongoing pressures on seabird food supplies, poor winter survival and increasingly extreme weather conditions.












“Unfortunately, this mirrors similar challenges that are affecting seabirds more widely.




“All of this underlines the importance of continued monitoring and conservation work at sites like the Isle of May NNR, where data and research are playing a vital role in helping us to understand these trends and respond.”




Puffins can spend up to eight months of the year out at sea, and only return to land in early spring to breed.








The birds generally mate for life, and pairs often return each year to the same nesting spot where the female lays a single egg which hatches into a puffling.


Rising ocean temperatures can affect the availability of food sources (Niall Carson/PA)
PA Archive




UKCEH said its long-term research shows that puffins have struggled with the impacts of climate change.

Storms in recent years have killed large numbers of birds, while rising ocean temperatures can reduce the availability of food sources for puffins – particularly sandeels.




UKCEH has been monitoring seabird colonies on the Isle of May for five decades.




Mark Newell, UKCEH’s field manager on the Isle of May, said: “We believe that the puffin population has recently suffered from a series of extreme climate events, including marine heat waves and intense storms affecting survival in three of the last five winters.












“The concern for puffins and other seabirds is that climate scientists are predicting an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme events in future.”

Digested week: Tom Tugendhat is a serious politician. What’s he doing in a Reform-lite Tory frontbench?

John Crace






Want to see how small the gene pool of Tory talent is? I give you Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. Also this week: Starmer’s Fomo, and telly wars





Monday
It’s the end of summer and Kemi Badenoch chose to mark the occasion with a reshuffle of her shadow cabinet. Her aim is apparently to get the Tories match fit in case Andy Burnham calls an early general election, but the vibes are much more rearranging the deckchairs on a sinking ship. After all, when the gene pool of talent is that small, there’s not much you can do. James Cleverly got the ball rolling by announcing he was planning to be the Conservative candidate for London mayor in two years’ time. He may have his work cut out. London is a liberal, multicultural city and unlikely to be won over by a party giving up on net zero and the European convention on human rights.

Cleverly’s replacement as shadow housing secretary is Katie Lam, who was only elected two years ago but has been desperate to attract attention by consistently saying the most offensive thing she can think of. This may not end well. Priti Patel’s departure as foreign secretary was no great surprise as she has always been a liability, but Kemi’s decision to appoint Tom Tugendhat in her place did raise eyebrows. Tom has always been from the One Nation side of the party and Kemi didn’t seem to realise that when he said: “If I had known Kemi was this good I wouldn’t have stood against her,” he had merely been joking. He is at least a serious politician in the way Priti never was, but you also can’t help wondering if he is really signed up to Kemi’s Reform-lite Tory agenda. Still, Tom has never been one to shy away from going to war with anyone, so he and Kemi will have something in common.


That just leaves the change of shadow chancellor. It goes without saying that Mel Stride had always been endearingly hopeless, but the choice of Andrew Griffith to take over is bewildering. The Tories always like to play up Griffith’s career in business, but what the rest of the country will be focusing on is that he was the co-author and defender of Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget. So maybe his economic judgment is not that sound after all. It should also be remembered that Griffith was Boris Johnson’s “net zero business champion” in 2020; something he and Kemi are also hoping to forget. Maybe the key to understanding Griffith is that he is just a career opportunist who doesn’t really believe in anything. In which case he may fit in just fine.

Fashion has become remarkably skilled at presenting small improvements as systemic change. A garment made with recycled fibres, a lower-impact collection or a resale scheme may suggest progress, yet the industry continues to manufacture clothes in quantities the planet cannot sustain.

An unprecedented El Nino event – when sea temperatures in tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average – is forecast to reach more than 3C in the coming months, making this year’s event “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.








El Nino creates a heightened risk of drought in the tropics, southern Africa and north-east Australia, while north-western Europe – including the UK – is likely to experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter, the forecaster said.




Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle has urged people to store supplies in case of extreme weather events.




And the Environment Secretary said people in the UK should prepare for the increased risk of national weather emergencies.




She told The Guardian: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Nino that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.




“It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.




“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t.











“So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”


Dame Angela Eagle has encouraged people to prepare (PA)
PA Wire




Professor Bill McGuire, professor emeritus of geophysical hazards, University College London, last month said the Met Office and other scientific forecasts “suggest that the world is in for one hell of a ride”.




“The astonishing and unprecedented amount of heat building across the eastern Pacific Ocean is all but certain to make this the most powerful El Nino in living memory – possibly even the biggest in several centuries,” he said.

Major Australian alpine resorts are closing their ski operations up to a month early after a winter that broke multiple records for heat with limited snow falls being washed away by rain.
Predictions in June that a building El Niño could combine with global heating for a challenging ski season came to pass, with seven resorts either already closed or announcing ski lifts will stop operating this weekend.

This week the Victorian resorts of Mount Buller, Mount Hotham and Falls Creek, together with Charlotte Pass in New South Wales, all announced ski operations would end this weekend.
The Victorian resort of Mount Baw Baw, the NSW resort at Selwyn and Tasmania’s Ben Lomond have already closed. Resorts typically aim to stay open until the first weekend of October.
 
 


Resorts blamed “challenging” weather conditions and lack of snowfall. Two other major NSW resorts at Perisher and Thredbo remain open.
“The season was frankly a shocker. This was the fourth disappointing season since 2020,” said Dr Andrew Watkins, a climate scientist and adjunct professor at the Monash University and a science adviser to the campaign group Protect our Winters.
“The problems were El Niño and climate change. It was not that dry this year, but the problem was the warmth. The heat just did us in.”
Watkins, who is also a keen skier, said winter temperatures had been too high and precipitation that might have fallen as snow, had instead fallen as rain.
“Rain is the natural enemy of a snowpack. It melts it and then washes it away,” he said.

He said that temperature rise would have been the difference between precipitation falling as rain instead of snow. “It would have been a bumper season if it had been 50 years ago,” he said.
The El Niño currently in place in the Pacific Ocean can promote hotter and drier temperatures in Australia’s south-east in winter and spring.
This week the bureau forecast the current El Niño would be the strongest on record and Australian scientists said climate change had made the strength of the event six times more likely.

More than half (53%) of Northern Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in the year to June – beating the level previously set in 2022.
And for the first time renewable generation has consistently exceeded non-renewable generation since January.
Even when imported electricity was taken into account, the amount of renewables equalled the previous record of 50%, set in 2022/23.
The Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the increasing level of renewable energy would help Northern Ireland "move away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices" .
Almost three-quarters (74%) of renewable electricity came from wind. Bioenergy – anaerobic digestion, incineration and fermentation – provided just under one-fifth (18%).
Solar energy provided 6%, landfill gas provided 1%, and hydro/tidal generation provided 1%.
Northern Ireland has a target of generating 80% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030.
The increase to 53% to June 2026 follows several years of reduced renewable generation.














Lower levels can be due to weather conditions.
There is also a high rate of dispatch down in Northern Ireland – when turbines are switched off because there is not enough demand for the power being generated.
That is to protect the grid which has a limit on the amount of renewable energy it can carry due to fluctuations.
But moving to more renewable energy is a critical part of the journey to net zero and the transition from fossil fuels.
The minister said the rising cost of fossil fuels globally was "impacting negatively" on both businesses and households, particularly those with lower incomes.
She added that increased levels of renewable electricity "move us away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices for the electricity we use".

British people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.
Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.

 As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies, Angela Eagle told the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of keeping supplies at home.

The environment secretary said: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

 “It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

 “If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”


El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.
The most recent data, from Monday, shows the temperature of the ocean at the heart of El Niño at 2.6C above the 30-year average. That is already close to the highest anomaly ever recorded in the satellite data era, 3.1C in 2015, with months to go before the peak is expected.
That peak is forecast to reach about 4C in November, according to the average of 14 different models. Zeke Hausfather, a climate analyst, said data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggested no El Niño had reached this level in the last millennium. Any temperature anomaly above 0.5C is classed as an El Niño.
The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be the hottest year ever recorded.

A blanket of toxic haze is enveloping parts of Indonesia and spreading into Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, as weeks-long wildfires continue to burn.
Millions of people across large swathes of South East Asia have been exposed to the smog, which in some areas has fuelled "acutely unhealthy" pollution more than 15 times the World Health Organization's recommended level.
Many of the ongoing fires have been burning across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo since mid-July – underpinned by a so-called Super El Niño that is exacerbating drought conditions.
Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires.
More than 12,000 of those cases are of children under the age of five.
Rizma Nur Fatimah, a 19-year-old teaching assistant at a school in Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan, told the BBC that the smog in her classroom had become so thick "you couldn't even see your own feet".
"Even inside the house, with everything closed, the haze still got in," she said. "We've been living with this since I was born. It's the same every year, so we've almost become resigned to it. But this year is worse."
Misbah, a 23-year-old mother from nearby Pengayuan village, said her three-year-old daughter had developed "a cough, a sore throat and a runny nose" during the haze.














Some 1,300 kilometres away, in the Philippine island province of Palawan, residents reported similar symptoms, including itchy eyes, nose and throat.
"We are now experiencing mild headaches," said Dr Precious Bañas-Melad. "My cousin who isn't allergic to anything started developing allergies. My husband is the first one who had itchy eyes and throat."
Malaysia, meanwhile, has reported rising cases of asthma and conjunctivitis amid worsening air quality nationwide as smoke continues to drift across the border.

Indonesia's forest and peatland fires are not a new phenomenon. Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.
Today, large-scale fires are often associated with the expansion of industrial plantations and other commercial land use. Environmental groups, researchers, and government investigations have repeatedly alleged that some companies use fire as a cheap and effective way to clear vast areas of land.
Some point out that while drought and El Niño conditions help fires spread, the severity of the haze is also linked to human activity. Drained peatlands, industrial timber estates and oil palm plantations can leave landscapes more vulnerable to burning, with fires often recurring in the same areas.

Gurjeet Grewal, CEO of Octopus Electric Vehicles, has led the calls for ministers to hold their nerve as the government considers changes to the rules that set rising targets for the proportion of zero-emission cars manufacturers must sell.

The final 2035 deadline, when all new cars and vans must be zero emission, is unchanged.





Car makers and the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders have pushed for more flexibility, arguing that the market has changed significantly since the rules were drawn up and warning about the pressure being put on manufacturers, jobs and investment.
Grewal takes the opposite view. “The ZEV mandate is working. It gives manufacturers confidence to invest and drivers confidence to switch to electric. Weakening it now would send exactly the wrong signal, just as EVs are becoming some of the best-value cars on the road,” he said.


He points to more than £41 billion of private-sector investment in the UK since 2020, along with more than £6 billion committed to charging infrastructure. He also says the public charging network has doubled to more than 120,000 chargers, while electric cars now account for more than a quarter of new-car sales.

Whilst no two events are the same, the current developing El Niño could mean a greater chance of stormy autumn weather in the UK. File image of Storm Herminia which hit the UK in January 2025



ByBen Rich
Lead Weather Presenter







21 August 2026
Updated 2 hours ago




El Niño is developing right now across the Pacific Ocean - thousands of miles away from the UK.
Its most profound impacts may well be centred around this area, with the increased risk of flooding and landslides in Peru and Ecuador and the threat of droughts and wildfires in Australia.
However the disruption caused to global wind patterns means the impacts will ripple right across the globe.
And the Met Office says the UK weather is likely to be affected, with the growing chance that autumn and early winter will be wet and stormy.
No two El Niños are the same - so, while it may increase the chance of certain types of weather occurring, this is not guaranteed.











El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office





21 August



Storms likely by November




"I have not seen an event like this developing in our forecasts before", said Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasts at the Met Office.
He says the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented in modern climate records.
As it approaches its peak by the end of 2026, its influence around the world will grow with effects spreading across the globe.
Professor Scaife says forecasters "already see signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
After a summer that looks set to be the UK's hottest on record and with the drought conditions that continue to grip large swathes of the country, a wet autumn sounds like good news.
However, we know that climate change is making increasingly intense rainfall more likely, and so these storms and downpours will also bring the threat of flooding.
Strong winds could also cause damage, transport disruption and power cuts.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.

Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?



Could it be a cold winter?




El Niño can be associated with cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.
The further forecasters look into the future the more uncertain the prospects become.
So while El Niño may increase the chance of cold weather early in 2027, this is not guaranteed.

Wildfires raging across Indonesia are pushing air quality to hazardous levels in cities hundreds of miles away, as officials warn the crisis is set to worsen with the El Niño weather pattern peaking this month.
Indonesian forestry minister Raja Juli Antoni said hotspots across Kalimantan and Sumatra had fallen by the end of August, but warned the fight was far from over. 
“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Nino," he said. "September is the main fight for us."





The wildfires burned more than 200,000 hectares of land across the country between January and July, including 95,000 hectares in July alone, as average temperatures for the month reached their highest in 35 years.
The fires are raging across a region that is home to endangered Bornean orangutans, leaving them writhing on the ground, fighting to even breathe, as air quality continues to plummet to hazardous levels and the haze spreads into neighbouring countries. 

Mr Antoni said “super El Nino" conditions were deepening the drought in the country, fuelling the fires, and that the disaster was largely man-made, with blazes deliberately set by individuals or companies to clear land for agriculture or other economic activity, a practice that remained common despite periodic government crackdowns.


The ministry had fined six forestry permit-holders over their alleged role in setting fires, he said, and a criminal investigation remained possible.

Air quality forecast shows hazardous levels (shown in purple) blanketing Malaysia and Indonesian Borneo as haze from the wildfires spreads across the region (Windy.com)
Satellite imaging had identified 42 companies holding land concessions with a high risk of wildfires, according to Rizal Irawan, a senior official at the Indonesian environment ministry. 



Police said last week they had arrested 72 people suspected of setting recent fires.
Authorities had deployed weather modification technology to trigger rainfall and used water bombing from aircraft to contain hotspots, Mr Antoni said. 
Cloudseeding and firefighting planes are now operating across five provinces of Borneo, much of it covered by fire-prone peatland that can smoulder underground for weeks even after a fire appears extinguished.





open image in gallery
Map shows poor air quality across Indonesia and nearby countries (IQAir)
In spite of such efforts, fires continue to surge in parts of Borneo. Hotspots in West Kalimantan nearly doubled in a single day at the end of August, rising by 3,553 to 7,377 while active fires increased by 88 to 104 and visibility fell below a kilometre, officials said. 





In Central Kalimantan, hotspots fell by 147 to 5,244 over the same period, though fire spots increased by 16 to 72.

articles.jina_text:
The world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027.
El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding.
Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said.




The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups.














The WMO - a UN agency - said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world."
El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere.
Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño.
In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event.
But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest.
This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin.












Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average.
Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast.
With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia.
It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change - leading to widespread coral bleaching and algae blooms, causing "unprecedented damage".

‘Supersizing before our eyes’: UN warns of record El Niño approaching


Event is likely to be largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into a world already in a climate crisis




The El Niño climate phenomenon is “supersizing before our eyes”, the UN has said. The event is near certain to shatter temperature records, according to the latest forecasts.
The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be the hottest year ever recorded.








What is a ‘super El Niño’ and what might it mean for the global climate?

Read more
The rising heat from the El Niño is already having impacts, from worsening wildfires in Indonesia to the weakening of vital monsoon rains in India. The impacts will spread globally, from greater fire risk in Australia to more intense floods in South America. The World Food Programme said in August that the El Niño was likely to push about 50 million people into acute hunger.
The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people, with the most extreme heatwave ever recorded hitting Europe this summer and leading to at least 35,000 deaths. The El Niño will ratchet up the impacts even further, with the scale of the event having been described as “truly mind-blowing” and a “Godzilla-level” event.
El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere. The most recent data, from Monday, shows the temperature of the ocean at the heart of El Niño at 2.6C above the 30-year average. That is already close to the highest anomaly ever recorded in the satellite data era, 3.1C in 2015, with months to go before the peak is expected.

That peak is forecast to reach about 4C in November, according to the average of 14 different models. Data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggest no El Niño has reached this level in the last millennium, said Zeke Hausfather, a climate analyst. Any temperature anomaly above 0.5C is classed as an El Niño.


A further concern is that recent research shows global heating is now intensifying El Niño cycles, which then in turn intensify the impacts of the climate crisis.

The confirmation of the extension of the Saraji mine, which digs and exports coal for steel making, comes after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, denied this week there was tension over Australia’s fossil fuel exports during talks with Pacific leaders.

In its application, BMA said it would likely have to clear 9.7 hectares of endangered koala habitat, 14.2 hectares of vulnerable ornamental snake habitat, 39 hectares of habitat of the vulnerable squatter pigeon and 3.1 hectares of threatened Brigalow woodland.

China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed


Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls




China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.
The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.

China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.


The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February.
How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.


View image in fullscreen
Wind turbines on the Yellow Sea coast of Yancheng, China. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA


The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.
This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.
In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.

An anti-Ulez protester is suspected to be behind the “scam” that saw Sir Sadiq Khan convicted and fined over an untaxed Nissan Micra. 




City Hall sources told The Standard there was a “big increase” in the number of vehicles being falsely registered to the Mayor of London around the time of the low emission zone being expanded to cover the entire capital in August 2023. 








In a criminal prosecution processed by the DVLA in Norwich, Sir Sadiq was found guilty by a magistrate last month of keeping an unlicensed vehicle. 




But he has insisted that the 24-year-old blue Micra does not belong to either him or Transport for London (TfL).


Sadiq Khan was been convicted over unpaid tax on an old Nissan Micra (stock picture)
GLA/Getty




A spokesman for the Mayor said: “This is a scam, which is a crime. It’s not the first time the Mayor has been victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. 




“Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware.”




He added that the DVLA was “urgently looking at getting the case reopened and with a view to withdrawing the prosecution”. 




The organisation will also investigate the false registration. 




It is understood that vehicles have been registered to Sir Sadiq on several other occasions since 2023, but this is the first time a case has reached court.












A magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the Single Justice Procedure in Herefordshire, convicted the Mayor in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs, and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.




Court documents show that DVLA letters addressed to the Mayor about the unpaid car tax bill were sent to Gordon Ramsay’s Bread Street Kitchen, Bar and Rooftop in Stratford, instead of the nearby TfL offices.

Climate experts warn that US Kalshi and Polymarket users are ‘gamifying disasters’ as they bet on events like heatwaves and daily temperatures




Online prediction markets, saturated by money staked on sport, crypto and politics, have now set their sights on a promising new area of growth: betting on the future livability of the planet itself.
The rise of gamified predictions on the unfolding climate crisis, and shorter-term weather forecasts, has been underscored by a new deal that allows Kalshi, a leading online financial exchange, to access data from the Weather Company, owner of the Weather Channel, to verify weather-related betting outcomes.

The weather is “one of the fastest-growing and most crucial categories” at Kalshi, the company said, with monetized predictions made by people, and bots, on weather and climate events growing 500% in the past year into a $1.1bn market.


“The long-term vision is to financialize everything and create a tradable asset out of any difference in opinion,” Tarek Mansour, co-founder of Kalshi, said of the company’s broader objectives last year.
Startlingly, Kalshi even claims that this gauge of public opinion can not only act as a financial hedge for businesses exposed to extreme weather, but also help shape the weather forecasts themselves. Kalshi’s betting markets will appear on the Weather Channel’s app, which is used by more than 330 million people worldwide.
“Given the severity of the climate crisis, it’s crucial for policymakers and the general public to have well-calibrated forecasting data about future climate impacts,” said a Kalshi spokesperson, citing a company study on how accurate its markets’ predictions are. Asked whether this meant Kalshi saw its weather markets as part of delivering well-calibrated forecasting data, the spokesperson said this was the case.
“Weather is the ultimate equalizer – it fundamentally affects everyone and everything,” the spokesperson said.
People visiting Kalshi or Polymarket, its main rival, can bet on weather predictions such as how hot it will be in certain places on a given day, as well as longer-term bets – from how many climate-fueled disasters the US will have, to whether the world will avoid catastrophic global heating, to how severe the die-off of corals in Hawaii will be.


You can even wager how far Lake Mead, the US’s largest reservoir and a crucial water source for the American west, will drop below its already record-low levels. Last year, amid ruinous wildfires in Los Angeles, there were $1.2m in bets laid on Polymarket on the extent of the fires, with one user posting that “volume so high in this market it cause another fire”.
While Polymarket’s international platform still hosts wildfire bets, US consumers are barred from accessing them. Kalshi meanwhile has never offered wildfire markets, citing “perverse incentives”.

Providers like Project:Camp offer emergency education and care to families in Washington state as climate change brings more destructive weather




One week after evacuating from the wildfires that devastated parts of this eastern Washington city, Mareesha Backman handed over her youngest son to a stranger and took her first deep breath of relief.
Spokane public schools was hosting what has become a growing part of disaster response: a day camp for children of survivors. Backman showed up that first day feeling “stunned”, she said: hot, poorly showered and underslept. Thanks to the camp’s volunteers, she was able to go to a doctor’s appointment, run errands and simply sit in the air-conditioned quiet of a friend’s home.

“ This is going to sound so corny,” she said, tearing up at the memory. “It kind of felt like the hug that I needed was there. And I was going to be OK, and there were people there who wanted to support us, help us, and I didn’t have to figure it out on my own any more.”



The wildfires, which began in early August, forced 60,000 people to evacuate and destroyed an estimated 920 structures. Spokane public schools reported that 169 students and 38 staff members lost their homes. So did an additional 20 students in the much smaller Nine Mile Falls school district, in a semi-rural wooded area north-west of the city.
With the effects of climate change intensifying, extreme weather is increasingly part of childhood. And, as fires, floods and storms rise, so too have networks and organizations to support children and families during such crises.
What’s called “education in emergencies”, or centering children’s needs in emergency response, is a best practice with its origins in international humanitarian aid, increasingly relevant here at home. Sarah Dryden-Peterson, who researches refugee education at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, said that beyond just providing childcare and safe supervision, education in emergencies ideally means “creating some predictable routines and structures so that the emergency and disaster can feel more understandable by young people”.

Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest


Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site




Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Have you ever wondered why it is that most houses in the UK are reliant on gas boilers? Not what’s stopping more people from replacing them with heat pumps, but instead why and how the gas boiler became so ubiquitous in the first place?
Arthur Downing, the author of the new book Power and the People: A History of British Energy, can tell you exactly why. “We only have boilers in our houses because of a state-owned enterprise that went into everybody’s home and installed natural gas-suitable appliances at no direct cost,” he says. The nationalised gas industry of the 1940s to the 1980s, which oversaw this huge project, was for three decades one of the “most dynamic, innovative, efficient industries in Britain”, Downing says. Yet few of us would use these terms to describe it as such now.

Instead, Britain’s electricity and gas industries are “fragile, fragmented, comically complicated and hopelessly dependent on imported fossil fuels”, Downing writes. On top of that, as consumers, we are facing soaring energy bills amid a cost of living crisis.


View image in fullscreen
Crowds admiring the electric lights on Victoria Docks, London, in the 19th century. From El Museo Popular, published 1887. Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty Images
Unearthing how this happened, by exploring the history of Britain’s energy industry, is the subject of Downing’s book. It’s one he lives and breathes – by day, Downing works as the director of strategy at Octopus Energy, the UK’s largest supplier of energy, but the book itself is written in a personal capacity.


Central to his argument is that this is a history a lot of us, even people working in the industry now, know little to nothing about. Yet it is instructive for the present, Downing argues, showing why we have the system we do – and, importantly, how we might change it for the better.
This summer’s string of climate crisis-driven heatwaves makes his book feel even more urgent. Although the UK has reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 50% compared with 1990 levels, Downing explains: “The second half of the journey will be much harder than the first. All the low-hanging fruits have been picked, like deindustrialising and switching from coal to gas.”

Good morning. This summer, datacentres have become targets of resistance across the world. Ever since the arrival of ChatGPT, big tech has been lobbying for the creation of enormous new facilities. Many governments claim they’re essential in any country that wants to cash in on AI.
Campaigners argue datacentres drain resources and exacerbate the climate crisis. The Scottish National Party has backed a moratorium on new developments; so has the Greens. The boom has been immense, and so has the backlash. Today’s newsletter explains why.

At First Edition, we’re keen on pushing the boundaries of frontier technologies (no luddites here), so today we’re trying something new: we’ve produced a video to accompany this newsletter, and you can watch more on the Guardian’s Instagram page. Let us know what you think by replying to this email. How’s that for innovation? Before you do, here are the headlines.
Five big stories
 
 
UK politics | Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years. 
 
Nepal-Tibet | A week on from the flash flooding disaster, authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples. 
 
Middle East | The US has launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counter strikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq, fuelling concerns about a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities. 
 
Ukraine | Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. 
 
US news | Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalation trade tensions between the US and Canada. 
In depth: ‘We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI’


View image in fullscreen

In August I attended a meeting of campaigners and councillors in the east London borough of Tower Hamlets, where the government has recently approved plans for a 5,200 sq metre datacentre on the site of an old brewery off Brick Lane. Summer of 2026 was UK’s hottest on record, Met Office says


Meteorologists say mean average temperature of 16.5C was made 130 times more likely by climate crisis




This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data, and the Met Office said the season’s mean temperature was made 130 times more likely by the climate crisis.
Record-breaking and back-to-back heatwaves have scorched much of Europe. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884. Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels.

The Met Office said an average mean UK temperature of 16.5C made this summer provisionally the warmest on record as well as the warmest season in a series going back to 1884. England, Wales and Northern Ireland broke their respective mean temperature records for summer while Scotland recorded its joint sixth hottest summer.


This is the second year in a row that temperature records have been broken, with 2025 and 2026 both the warmest UK summers since records began.
The infamous summer of 1976 is now the seventh warmest on record in terms of mean temperature.
Katie White, the minister for climate transition, said it was a “brutal reminder that we’re not waiting for climate change to arrive in Britain, we’re living in the middle of it. With kids too hot to sleep, families worrying about older relatives, farmers watching fields dry out, and firefighters and our armed forces battling wildfires, we’ve all woken up to a reality none of us wants for the people and places we love.”


View image in fullscreen
Smoke rising from a major wildfire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, in late July.  Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA


England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone.
A study conducted by Met Office scientists showed this summer’s record-breaking heat was made about 130 times more likely because of human-induced climate change. The Met Office’s climate projections indicate that UK summers will continue to become hotter.
The Met Office’s head of climate attribution, Dr Mark McCarthy, said: “The summer of 2026 has been remarkable and is an example of the extremes we can expect to see more frequently as a consequence of human-induced climate change.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to “meet the climate challenge” as he confirmed he would attend the annual UN climate summit in November.




Addressing MPs for the first time as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham said he would attend the Cop 31 meeting in Antalya, on Turkey’s southern coast, as his predecessors had done.








Pointing to last week’s devastating floods in Nepal, he told MPs: “This is what the climate crisis looks like.




“We have just ourselves experienced what is likely to have been the hottest summer on record.




“This Government will meet the climate challenge, and I can confirm to the House that I will attend Cop 31 in Turkey in November.”








His commitment to attend Cop 31 came only a few hours after provisional figures from the Met Office suggested 2026 was the UK’s hottest summer since records began.




The average temperature across June, July and August was 16.5C, beating the previous high of 16.1C set only last year.




This summer was also the first to see three separate days where temperatures exceeded 37C as parts of the country suffered as many as five heatwaves thought to have caused thousands of deaths.











Green Party MP Adrian Ramsey said the summer’s high temperatures required “a response that meets the needs of the moment and our future”, urging Mr Burnham not to approve new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.

Five heatwaves between May and August left the majority of the country in drought and have sparked wildfires and travel disruption.
The UK recorded a mean average temperature across June, July and August of 16.5C, beating the previous seasonal high of 16.1C set last year, the Met Office said. 





The forecaster previously suggested the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record, provided temperatures remained around average for the rest of August, and it is expected the final figures for the month will break the previous record.
Despite a cooler end to August, areas of high pressure have dominated, with dry conditions from continental Europe causing temperatures to rise.

The first heatwave in May also broke that month’s temperature record by more than 2C, while parts of the UK experienced a three-week heatwave in July and August.
